Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

with preposition

the tool or the part of the body used

also with a knife, with a spoon, with your hands, using

classical

Cato Agr. 45.1: malleō aut mateolā adigitō
Varr. RR 1.55.2: harundine potius quam perticā feriantur

cāsus ablātīvus

construction: the tool in the ablative, with no preposition

with (a tool, a hand)

Latin does not use cum with a tool: cultrō secāre, to cut with a knife; manū tangere, to touch with the hand. Cum with a thing means having it along (see “with”, in company).

Other words

  • ūtor, ūtī, ūsus sum — use (a tool, one’s hands)

    verb, third conjugation, deponent, with the ablative · also used · classical · Cic. Fin. 5.42: manibus ūtuntur

    For “with” meaning “using”: ūtere furcillā, use your fork.

Examples

  • cum tāleam dēmittēs, pede tāleam opprimitō. sī parum dēscendet, malleō aut mateolā adigitō

    when you set the cutting, press it down with your foot; if it doesn’t go deep enough, drive it in with a hammer or a malletCato Agr. 45.1

  • quae manū tangī nōn poterunt, ita quatī dēbent, ut harundine potius quam perticā feriantur; gravior enim plāga medicum quaerit

    the ones that can’t be reached by hand should be knocked down with a reed rather than a pole; a heavier blow calls for a doctorVarr. RR 1.55.2

  • manibus siccīs, cum ūtī volēs, sūmitō

    when you want to use them, take them out with dry handsCato Agr. 117

  • pōnētur digitīs tenendus ūnctīs nigrā cōliculus virēns patellā

    a green cabbage sprout will be served on a black dish, to be held in oily fingersMart. 5.78.6–7

  • cum autem paulum firmitātis accessit, et animō ūtuntur et sēnsibus cōnītunturque, ut sēsē ērigant, et manibus ūtuntur et eōs agnōscunt, ā quibus ēducantur

    when they have grown a little stronger, babies use their minds and senses, try to stand up, use their hands, and know the people who bring them upCic. Fin. 5.42

See also with, by, tool.
